# The Value of Disagreement: Why the Best Meetings Don't End in Consensus

## Rethinking What a Successful Meeting Looks Like

There is a common assumption, woven into how most organizations operate, that a good meeting is one where everyone walks out nodding. We celebrate alignment. We praise teams that "get on the same page." A meeting that ends in consensus feels productive; a meeting that ends in argument feels like a failure, or at least an unfinished piece of business.

But this assumption deserves scrutiny. Agreement, it turns out, can be deceptive. Sometimes people agree because they have genuinely converged on the truth. But often they agree because someone senior spoke first and no one wanted to contradict them, because everyone is tired and wants to go home, because the topic is genuinely murky and nodding is easier than thinking, or because the words being agreed to are vague enough to mean different things to different people. That last one is especially dangerous: two people can leave a room both believing a decision was made, only to discover weeks later that they made *different* decisions.
